paper.title: Dynamic evolution of quality attributes, flavor formation, and protein structural changes in high-moisture meat analogues during marination and pasteurization.
paper.abstract: Currently, research on the dynamic evolution of flavor and quality in high-moisture meat analogs (HMMAs) remains insufficient. This study aims to elucidate how marination modulates texture and flavor compound profiles of HMMAs, while also examining the combined effects of marination and subsequent pasteurization on flavor substance dynamics. Continuous marination at 95 °C for 30 min and pasteurization at 75 °C for 15 min were performed, with samples characterized at different time points during marination (0-30 min) and pasteurization (0-15 min). The quality of HMMAs generally showed a trend of initial optimization followed by deterioration with extended marination time. 20 min marination resulted in low hardness (2102N), high cohesiveness (0.96) and chewiness (20,149 N), achieving the highest denaturation temperature (Tp) value of 124.97 °C. With extended marination time, the total content of volatile flavor substances in HMMAs showed an upward trend, with a significant increase in spice flavor components and anethole content rose from 0.686 ng/g to 1.203 ng/g. However, pasteurization caused the loss of most volatile flavor substances, with significantly decreased 2-butylfuran, which contributed to a pleasant cooked flavor perception. 12 min pasteurization led to ideal coordination of volatile flavor components, effectively mitigating fat oxidation induced by heat accumulation and balancing the spice flavor while meeting the product's microbial safety indicators. The results deepen insights into post-extrusion processing of HMMAs and provide actionable technical support for the coordinated control of marination and pasteurization in industrial plant-based meat manufacturing.

paper.title: Tea polyphenols at the sensory-functional interface: Bitterness, astringency, bioactivity and modulation through macromolecular interactions.
paper.abstract: Tea polyphenols, especially catechins, contribute to bitterness and astringency while also being widely investigated for potential health-related bioactivities. This sensory-functional tension affects consumer acceptance, product formulation and the development of tea-based functional foods. Although sensory studies and health-oriented studies have both advanced, their relationship remains insufficiently examined. This review examines them through a polyphenol-macromolecule interaction framework. In the oral cavity, such interactions help explain salivary protein aggregation, lubrication loss and astringent mouthfeel. In digestive and systemic settings, related binding events may contribute to enzyme modulation, membrane association, nutrient bioaccessibility and other biological activities. Of particular interest is the galloyl group, which has been associated with interactions with biological targets while also increasing bitter taste receptor activation and binding to salivary proteins. These effects are conditional rather than fixed, because processing, formulation, fermentation and aging can redirect polyphenol structure, availability and interaction behavior. This review integrates evidence on molecular perception, sensory evaluation, matrix effects, health-related activity and transformation strategies, and considers how bitterness and astringency might be reduced without eliminating the compounds with potential bioactivity.

paper.title: Non-invasive oral magnetoelectric vagus nerve neuromodulation for Parkinson's disease therapy.
paper.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation has shown promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in progressive neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease. However, its invasive nature introduces procedural and device-related risks. Here we introduce a magnetoelectric particulate system for oral delivery and non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation through the gut. The system comprises a magneto-responsive nickel ferrite core and a piezoelectric barium titanate shell, conjugated with capsaicin to specifically target TRPV1 receptors, ensuring effective adherence to the stomach lining after oral administration. Upon magnetic field stimulation, the particles generate electrical pulses that activate vagal afferent fibres, engaging the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem via the gut-brain axis. This activation enhances norepinephrine production in the locus coeruleus and dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra. Vagal efferent activation triggers the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, mitigating both neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation. This non-invasive approach demonstrates potential for alleviating motor symptoms and non-motor anxiety in Parkinson's disease, offering valuable insights into its mechanisms and clinical applications.

paper.title: Patient-reported oral complaints during cancer treatment: Dietary consequences, supportive care, and self-management in a cross-sectional survey.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oral complaints are common during cancer treatment and may interfere with eating and perceived quality of life. However, patient-reported evidence addressing dental and gingival complaints, xerostomia, taste alterations, counselling, and self-management remains limited.

METHODS: We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional survey among adults in Germany with current or previous oncological treatment using paper-based and online questionnaires (January-June 2025). Analyses were based on valid responses for each item and included descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square tests, linear-by-linear association tests, 95% confidence intervals for selected key prevalence estimates, and exploratory multivariable logistic regression sensitivity analyses adjusted for age and gender.

RESULTS: The survey included 222 patients. New, additional, or worsening dental and gingival complaints during cancer treatment were reported by 41.9% (83/198; 95% CI 35.3-48.9%) of respondents. Xerostomia was reported by 56.6% (120/212; 95% CI 49.9-63.1%) and taste alterations by 68.0% (138/203; 95% CI 61.3-74.0%). Self-reported reduced food intake attributed to dental or gingival complaints was reported by 27.9% (57/204; 95% CI 22.2-34.5%), while 25.0% (46/184; 95% CI 19.3-31.7%) reported perceived quality-of-life impairment attributed to these complaints. In exploratory sensitivity analyses adjusted for age and gender, new, additional, or worsening complaints remained associated with reduced food intake (adjusted OR 7.85, 95% CI 3.70-16.62) and perceived quality-of-life impairment (adjusted OR 15.25, 95% CI 5.81-40.06). Among participants with xerostomia, the proportion reporting reduced food intake increased from 5.1% among those with no xerostomia-related eating difficulty to 91.7% among those with severe difficulty (p < 0.001). Overall, 43.1% (87/202; 95% CI 36.4-50.0%) reported receiving support or counselling regarding oral health.

CONCLUSIONS: In this recruited sample, oral complaints during cancer treatment were common and were associated with eating-related burden and perceived quality-of-life impairment. These exploratory associations persisted after limited adjustment for age and gender but do not establish causality. Fewer than half of respondents reported receiving oral-health counselling, although perceived helpfulness was high among recipients, suggesting a potential gap in the reach of such support. These findings support prospective evaluation of repeated, function-oriented oral-health assessment and appropriate dental or nutritional referral rather than demonstrating the effectiveness of these approaches.

paper.title: Oral Adverse Drug Reactions in Patients Receiving Polypharmacy: A Prospective Interdisciplinary Case Series.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Polypharmacy in older adults markedly increases the risk of adverse drug reactions (ADRs). While the systemic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic consequences of polypharmacy are extensively documented, the oral cavity remains an under-evaluated site for both mucosal and functional drug toxicity. Drug-induced oral manifestations range from dysgeusia and xerostomia to gingival overgrowth, lichenoid reactions, erythema multiforme, opportunistic infection, angioedema, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, and they meaningfully impair oral health-related quality of life. This case series was undertaken to characterize oral ADRs in patients on polypharmacy through a targeted, interdisciplinary pharmacovigilance approach. This study aims to identify and characterize the spectrum of oral ADRs in patients exposed to polypharmacy, determine the drug classes most frequently implicated, and assess the causality of each reaction using a standardized probability scale.

METHODS: This prospective, observational case series was conducted over six months at a tertiary care teaching hospital. Ten adult patients taking five or more concurrent systemic medications who developed new-onset oral lesions or functional oral impairment were enrolled after written informed consent. The evaluation was delivered through an interdisciplinary collaboration led by a dentist, together with the Departments of Pharmacology and Community Medicine. Comprehensive medication reconciliation and a structured oral examination were performed, and causality was assessed using the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale.

RESULTS: Ten patients (mean age 67.8 years; 60% male) taking between five and eight concurrent medications were evaluated. The most frequent oral ADRs were functional salivary impairment (xerostomia, 20%) and structural modification (gingival overgrowth, 20%). The agents most often implicated were antihypertensives (calcium channel blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors), anticholinergics, and anticonvulsants. Causality assessment classified eight reactions (80%) as probable and two (20%) as possible; none was classified as definite or doubtful. Severity assessment using the Modified Hartwig and Siegel scale classified most reactions as moderate (70%), and preventability assessment using the Schumock and Thornton criteria identified over half as probably preventable (60%).

CONCLUSION: Polypharmacy necessitates vigilant, proactive monitoring for oral mucosal and functional toxicity. Active interdisciplinary collaboration between a dentist, pharmacologists, and community medicine physicians can facilitate recognition and assessment of suspected oral ADRs, early mitigation of drug-induced oral morbidity, and improved patient care.

paper.title: Intestinal epithelial CSE-derived H2S alleviates food allergy via modulating the IL-25/ILC2 axis.
paper.abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S), an endogenous gasotransmitter, has garnered increasing attention for its role in modulating immune responses and intestinal barrier function. In this study, diminished jejunal H2S levels and expression of its synthesizing enzyme cystathionine gamma-lyase (CSE) in intestinal epithelium were observed in ovalbumin (OVA)-induced food allergic mice. CSE deficiency aggravated OVA-induced food allergy by activating the IL-25/ILC2 axis and enhancing type 2 immune responses, effects that were reversed by exogenous H2S supplementation. Furthermore, H2S treatment suppressed intestinal epithelial cell-derived IL-25 expression by inhibiting c-Jun. IL-25 neutralization attenuated ILC2-driven type 2 immune responses and alleviated allergic symptoms in OVA-challenged CSE-knockout (Cse -/- ) mice. Moreover, ILC2 inhibition diminished type 2 cytokine production and disrupted the IL-25 feedback loop, thereby ameliorating food allergy in Cse -/- mice. These findings highlight that intestinal epithelial CSE-derived H2S alleviates food allergy via the IL-25/ILC2 axis and serves as a potential therapeutic target for allergic diseases.

paper.title: Current and Emerging Inflammatory Biomarkers of Chronic Rhinosinusitis.
paper.abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis, CRS, is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease of the sinonasal mucosa. Although the traditional distinction between chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, CRSwNP, and chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps, CRSsNP, remains clinically useful, it does not fully reflect the biological complexity of the disease. Current biomarker approaches are often limited by incomplete correspondence between systemic markers and the local sinonasal inflammatory microenvironment, making integrated assessment increasingly relevant for endotyping, prognosis, therapeutic selection, and longitudinal monitoring. This narrative review summarizes established and emerging inflammatory biomarkers in CRS, with particular emphasis on CRSwNP. Established or clinically accessible biomarkers, including blood eosinophils, tissue eosinophilia, total IgE, FeNO, olfactory testing, endoscopic scores, radiological findings, and patient-reported outcomes, are discussed together with emerging or mainly translational biomarkers such as epithelial alarmins, Galectin-10, Charcot-Leyden crystals, extracellular traps, mucins, local IgE, mast cells, neutrophils, microbial biomarkers, biofilm-related patterns, and tissue remodeling mediators. No single biomarker appears sufficient to guide personalized management alone. An integrated framework combining molecular, cellular, epithelial, microbial, functional, radiological, endoscopic, and patient-reported data may provide a more accurate assessment of disease activity and therapeutic response. Within this framework, nasal cytology and Clinical-Cytological Grading, CCG, represent minimally invasive, repeatable, and practical tools that directly reflect local inflammation and may support endotypic stratification, recurrence risk assessment, treatment selection, and follow-up in severe and recurrent CRSwNP.

paper.title: Simulation-Based Certification for Mastoidectomy Surgery.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To design and evaluate a simulation-based certification pathway for mastoidectomy using VR simulation and 3D-printed temporal bone models. An adapted Learning Curve-Cumulative Summation (LC-CUSUM) method was used to establish a credible competency threshold. We aimed to examine training effects, item-level performance patterns, and transfer to cadaveric dissection.

METHODS: Seven senior residents and early-career otologic surgeons completed a structured curriculum consisting of VR simulation training followed by 3D-printed model drilling. Competency thresholds were defined using an adapted LC-CUSUM design requiring 4 consecutive high scoring performances (≥22/26 points on a modified Welling Scale, without damage to the lateral semicircular canal or facial nerve). Cadaveric mastoidectomy performance was assessed at baseline, after VR simulation training, and after 3D-printed training. Linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate changes in cadaver performance and predictors of final outcomes. Item-level performance was explored across modalities.

RESULTS: Five of seven participants (71%) met VR simulation certification criteria, and four (57%) met certification criteria on 3D-printed models. Cadaver performance improved significantly across tests (baseline 14.1; post-VR 15.8; post-3D-print, ie, final, 16.3 points; P = .02). Certified participants scored significantly higher on the final cadaver test than non-certified participants (17.1 vs 13.7 points; P < .001). Item level analysis identified persistent challenges (eg, performance related to sigmoid sinus, tegmen, mastoid tip, chorda tympani) and simulation to cadaver discrepancies.

CONCLUSION: A simulation-based certification pathway for mastoidectomy is feasible and produces measurable improvements in cadaveric performance. Achieving certification in both VR simulation and 3D-printed modalities was necessary for any cadaveric passing performance, supporting the use of mastery learning with LC-CUSUM-based thresholds in otologic surgical training.

paper.title: Mechanisms Underlying Region-Specific Vulnerability and Resistance to Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in the Central Nervous System.
paper.abstract: Selective neuronal vulnerability is a hallmark of ischemic injury in the central nervous system (CNS), yet the mechanisms underlying regional differences in neuronal survival and degeneration remain incompletely understood. Cerebral ischemia from ischemic stroke or cardiac arrest triggers a complex cascade of metabolic failure, excitotoxic signaling, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammatory responses that collectively determine neuronal fate. Notably, neuronal degeneration follows highly specific anatomical patterns rather than uniformly throughout the CNS. Classical experimental studies have shown that hippocampal cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) pyramidal neurons undergo delayed neuronal death after transient global ischemia, whereas neighboring CA3 neurons remain relatively resistant. Similar heterogeneity is observed in other regions, including the olfactory bulb and spinal cord, where mitral cells and dorsal horn neurons exhibit relative resistance to ischemic injury. Accumulating evidence indicates that selective vulnerability arises from the interplay of multiple molecular and cellular mechanisms, including excitotoxic glutamatergic signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neurovascular unit dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory responses. In addition, structural and circuit-level determinants such as hippocampal connectivity and regional neurovascular organization further influence neuronal susceptibility to ischemic stress. This review integrates evidence from experimental and clinical studies to examine the mechanisms underlying neuronal vulnerability and resistance across the CNS. Particular emphasis is placed on the interplay between neuronal metabolism, glial responses, and neurovascular regulation in shaping regional injury patterns. Understanding these mechanisms may provide important insights for the development of mechanism-based neuroprotective strategies targeting selectively vulnerable neuronal populations.

paper.title: A preconceptional stress model identifies thalamostriatal substrates of intergenerational vulnerability.
paper.abstract: Antenatal depression affects up to 20% of pregnancies worldwide and is associated with increased neuropsychiatric vulnerability in offspring, yet the enduring behavioural, neuroanatomical, and molecular features associated with maternal mood disturbance remain incompletely characterized. Offspring of SIR dams exhibited robust anxiety-like behaviours across multiple paradigms. High-resolution ex vivo structural magnetic resonance imaging revealed reduced relative volumes of the thalamus and striatum, together with relative expansion of gustatory/visceral and visual cortices. Multivariate analyses identified a pattern of thalamostriatal and other regional volume differences that covaried with behavioural impairment. Diffusion tensor imaging further identified region-specific elevations in fractional anisotropy, consistent with persistent differences in brain microstructure. Transcriptomic profiling of the thalamus revealed widespread, sex-dependent differences in gene expression, implicating pathways related to synaptic organization, protein synthesis, neuronal plasticity, and myelination. Exploratory DNA-methylation analyses identified nominal, sex-dependent pathway enrichments that did not survive false-discovery-rate correction. Together, these findings show that maternal stress beginning before pregnancy leaves a persistent imprint on offspring brain structure, microstructure, and epigenetic regulation, converging on the thalamus as a central hub of intergenerational vulnerability. This work establishes SIR as a translationally relevant model of depression that predates conception and provides integrated MRI- and molecular-level biomarkers for dissecting mechanisms and informing early preventive strategies.

paper.title: The neural basis of flavour-nutrient learning.
paper.abstract: Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour-nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour-nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

paper.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila.
paper.abstract: Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1-6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male's visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta's strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

paper.title: Identification and validation of RNA-binding protein-associated biomarkers in esophageal cancer.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Esophageal cancer (ESCA) is highly prevalent globally, but the role of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) in it remains unclear.

paper.title: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder as a model of early neurodegeneration: challenges for research and clinical diagnosis.
paper.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) has evolved from a descriptive parasomnia to a clinically informative model for studying early neurodegenerative processes, particularly within the spectrum of α-synucleinopathies. Defined by the loss of REM sleep atonia and the emergence of dream enactment behaviors, RBD reflects dysfunction of brainstem circuits that normally suppress motor output during dreaming. Longitudinal evidence indicates that many individuals with isolated RBD eventually develop neurodegenerative disease, most commonly Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or, less frequently, multiple system atrophy, positioning RBD among the most specific clinical markers of prodromal synucleinopathy currently recognized. Mechanistic studies suggest that RBD arises from instability within distributed REM sleep regulatory networks involving dopaminergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, and cholinergic systems. This network dysfunction may precede classic motor and cognitive symptoms and can be accompanied by early abnormalities in neurophysiology, imaging, cognition, olfaction, autonomic function, and molecular biomarkers. These findings support a model in which RBD may represent one of the earliest clinically accessible manifestations of a multisystem neurodegenerative process, although anatomical origin, propagation patterns, and phenoconversion trajectories vary across patients. Despite these advances, clinical management remains largely symptomatic, and key challenges persist in diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic counselling, and therapeutic development. A broader clinical framework is therefore needed, in which RBD is not viewed solely as an isolated sleep disorder but also as a potential marker of early neurodegeneration in appropriately characterized patients. Integrating polysomnography with multimodal biomarkers and network-based models of disease may refine risk stratification and support the development of targeted interventions at earlier stages of neurodegenerative disease.

paper.title: Sustained metabolic defense and male-specific volatile repellence shape tea plant-Helopeltis theivora interactions.

Meanwhile, phenylalanine accumulation and auxin metabolic remodeling increased progressively with infestation pressure. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed coordinated activation of the phenylpropanoid-flavonoid pathway as a central metabolic defense module. Pinobanksin-3-acetate accumulated substantially and was identified as a potential chemical component contributing to tea resistance. In parallel, feeding-induced (E)-β-ocimene emission increased significantly and elicited dose-dependent behavioral avoidance in adult male H. theivora, suggesting that this volatile may function as an olfactory cue for assessing host defensive status. Together, our findings reveal a complex ecological consequence of herbivore-induced defense: tea plants enhance metabolic resistance while simultaneously releasing volatile signals that may influence herbivore host-selection behavior. These insights provide potential chemical targets for developing sustainable pest management strategies through manipulation of plant defense pathways and insect behavioral responses.

paper.title: Neuroinflammation is an early pathological process in a mouse model of prodromal Parkinson's disease.
paper.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Approximately 90% of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients exhibit olfactory deficits, which often precedes motor symptoms by years, and are a robust predictor for PD and subsequent cognitive decline. Pathological changes in the PD olfactory system, particularly α-synuclein (αSyn) pathology in the olfactory bulb (OB) and severe involvement of the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), are distinct from normal aging. However, the causal link between αSyn aggregation and functional impairment, potentially involving cytotoxicity and neuroinflammation, remains elusive. To investigate these early pathological events, we utilized a prodromal PD model that we have previously characterized, involving the unilateral OB injection of αSyn pre-formed fibrils (PFF) in wild-type mice. This triggers the transneuronal spread of pathogenic αSyn, and olfactory dysfunction starting at 1-month post-injections. Here we report on neuropathological and inflammatory events 1-3 month following injection of PFFs into the OB. Following PFF injection, αSyn pSer129 pathology progressively accumulated bilaterally in the AON and ipsilateral in the piriform cortex (PCX) over three months. Stereological quantification revealed no significant neuronal loss in the AON or PCX during this 1-3 month interval, indicating that olfactory impairment precedes overt neurodegeneration. Instead, we identified the upregulation of pro-inflammatory genes ( Il- 1β and Il-6 ), significant microglial reactivity, and sustained astrogliosis within olfactory structures. These findings identify neuroinflammation as a key early mediator linking αSyn pathology to olfactory dysfunction in the absence of neuronal loss. This suggests a critical window for therapeutic intervention and highlights neuroinflammatory markers as potential biomarkers for the prodromal phase of PD.

Progressive αSyn pSer129 spreading. Pathological αSyn pSer129 progressively spreads transneuronally from the injection site in the OB to secondary olfactory structures (AON and PCX) within 1 to 3 months. Early Microglial Reactivity. The spreading of αSyn pSer129 pathology rapidly induces microglial reactivity, which is prominent at the 1- and 2-month time points. Persistent Astrogliosis. Astrogliosis is also an early and persistent component of the neuroinflammatory response, starting at 1 month and remaining detectable through 3 months, suggesting a sustained inflammatory environment.

paper.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Intranasal Opioids vs. Intravenous Morphine for Acute Moderate-to-Severe Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intranasal (IN) opioids may provide noninvasive analgesia without delays associated with intravenous (IV) access, but their efficacy and safety vs. IV morphine remain uncertain.

OBJECTIVES: To synthesize randomized evidence comparing IN opioids with IV morphine for acute moderate-to-severe pain.

METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults or children with acute moderate-to-severe pain in emergency, prehospital, procedural, or postoperative settings. Eligible trials directly compared IN opioids with IV morphine. The primary outcome was change in pain score from baseline at 20 and 30 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events. Outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMD) or risk ratios (RR) using random-effects models.

RESULTS: Ten RCTs involving 1164 participants were included. IN opioids showed comparable analgesic efficacy to IV morphine at 20 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.24 to 0.14; p = 0.59; I² = 11.94%) and 30 minutes (SMD = -0.05, 95% CI: -0.24 to 0.15; p = 0.64; I² = 0.00%). Rescue analgesia was comparable (RR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.81-1.25; p = 0.98). No significant differences were observed in overall adverse events, serious adverse events, respiratory complications, hypotension, gastrointestinal events, dizziness, or rhinorrhea. Dysgeusia was borderline increased.

CONCLUSION: IN opioids provide analgesic efficacy comparable to IV morphine at 20 and 30 minutes, with no clear increase in systemic adverse events. Larger trials should confirm safety for rare serious events and optimize dosing.

paper.title: Sensorimotor behaviour from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome.
paper.abstract: Connectomes now map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behaviour follows from the wiring is unknown. Two fixed rules join them: odours and looming objects drive sensory neurons, and motor neurons move the legs. Alone, the network passes a signal to the motor neurons it is known to drive when the pathway supplies about 2% or more of their input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to 95% of the odour sources. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches 18%, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none, so navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odour into avoidance, which requires the pairing and is odour-specific once one olfactory synapse class is scaled. An untrained connectome thus supports a behaviour and its learned reversal, and the pathways it cannot drive mark what the diagram leaves out.

paper.title: Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder as a Prodromal Manifestation of Alpha-Synucleinopathies.
paper.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia in which patients physically act out their dreams due to loss of the normal muscle paralysis that occurs during REM sleep. It is now recognized that isolated RBD (iRBD) is strongly associated with future development of α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). It is seen that most patients with polysomnography-confirmed iRBD eventually develop a clinically defined synucleinopathy, often after a long symptom-free interval. This long prodromal phase makes iRBD a unique clinical model for studying the earliest stages of neurodegeneration, before the onset of clear motor or cognitive disability. α-synuclein pathology frequently begins in the lower brainstem and autonomic nervous system, affecting REM sleep regulatory circuits early in the disease process. As pathology spreads, dopaminergic, cholinergic, and cortical systems become involved, leading to the gradual emergence of motor, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms. As a result, many individuals with iRBD exhibit subtle non-motor features such as hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, anxiety, and mild cognitive changes years before a formal neurological diagnosis is made. Recent advances have improved the ability to identify patients at the highest risk of near-term phenoconversion. Quantitative measures of REM sleep without atonia, dopamine transporter imaging, autonomic testing, and emerging molecular biomarkers, including α-synuclein seed amplification assays, have shown promise in risk stratification. In addition, cognitive changes may occur earlier than previously recognized, particularly in patients with iRBD who also demonstrate hyposmia or dopaminergic dysfunction. Management of RBD remains largely symptomatic and focuses on injury prevention and sleep stabilization. While clonazepam and melatonin remain first-line therapies, alternative treatments including sodium oxybate, serotonergic agents, cannabinoids, and modulation of the gut-brain axis through probiotic supplementation have also been explored. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge regarding the clinical features, mechanisms, biomarkers, and management of RBD as a prodromal manifestation of α-synucleinopathies, with emphasis on its importance for early diagnosis and future disease-modifying research.

KEGG pathway enrichment-an indirect inference from volatile end-products-indicated that terpenoid backbone, monoterpenoid, and sesquiterpenoid/triterpenoid biosynthesis are the principal routes plausibly governing tissue-specific aroma formation. These findings establish a foundation for wampee quality assessment, cultivar authentication, and flavor-oriented breeding.

PURPOSE: To characterize the neuroimaging spectrum of nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (NBCCS), with particular emphasis on cerebellar abnormalities.

Dural calcification was detected in 13 of 16 evaluable patients (81.3%), while maxillary and/or mandibular odontogenic keratocysts were present in 10 of 13 patients with dedicated maxillofacial computed tomography (76.9%). Intracranial neoplasms included two meningiomas and one previously treated medulloblastoma.

CONCLUSION: Cerebellar abnormalities, particularly macrocerebellum and cerebellar dysplasia, may be underrecognized components of the neuroimaging phenotype of NBCCS. Awareness of these findings may support syndromic recognition and appropriate clinical and genetic evaluation.

paper.title: A novel behavioral paradigm to model hypermemory-like features in rats.

BACKGROUND: Episodic memory is essential to everyday life and personal identity, but its dysfunction can affect mental health. Translational animal models for investigating these dysfunctions remain limited, particularly for abnormally enhanced memories.

NEW METHOD: We developed a paradigm to induce hypermemory-like features in adult male and female rats using object recognition (OR) and object location (OL) tasks mimicking the rumination-like component of hypermemory. During odor-context association training, rats explored two identical objects with a cinnamon scent. Over the following 6 h, they received 12 brief re-exposures to cinnamon odor, an odor-free stimulus, or a novel neutral odor to control for nonspecific effects. Re-exposure to the learning-associated odor was designed to promote iterative consolidation of spatial memory. After 24 h, memory was assessed under odor-free conditions.

RESULTS: Odor re-exposure selectively enhanced OL memory in both sexes, whereas OR memory remained unaffected. Neither total object exploration nor locomotion was altered. Enhanced spatial memory was accompanied by increased ventral hippocampal c-Fos expression in both sexes.

COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Unlike conventional memory paradigms, which primarily assess memory impairment or enhancement, our approach models the persistence of otherwise short-term memories through repeated exposure to a learning-associated cue.

CONCLUSIONS: Our protocol is designed to model key features theoretically associated with hyperfunctional episodic memory, using repeated olfactory reactivation to mimic rumination and memory replay hypothesized to contribute to enhanced autobiographical memory in HSAM. This simple paradigm provides a novel translational tool for investigating the behavioral and neurobiological mechanisms underlying enhanced memory consolidation and memory persistence.

paper.abstract: Bud-leaf yellow tea is known for its chestnut-sweet aroma, yet its key odorants and formation mechanism remain unclear. Using a sensomics approach, seven key odorants were characterized, including 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine, 3-methylbutanal, and dimethyl sulfide, with 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine being the major contributor (recombination correlation r = 0.909). 2-Ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine (odor activity value = 53.3, flavor dilution = 1024) and dimethyl sulfide (odor activity value = 422.4, flavor dilution = 256) were identified as major contributors, with dimethyl sulfide dominating the chestnut note and 2-Ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine enhancing the sweet dimension. Across Meizhan, FudingDabaicha and Echa 10, 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine was undetectable before yellowing, peaked during yellowing (14.92 μg/L, p < 0.05), and was moisture-dependent, with 25% post-fixation moisture giving the highest chestnut-sweet score. In vitro, β-alanine + D-arabinose produced 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine via the Maillard reaction. Thus, 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine is the yellowing-specific key chestnut-sweet odorant in bud-leaf yellow tea, enabling moisture-based process control.

paper.title: The lost scent of excitation: dissociation between cognitive desire and physical arousal in Kallmann syndrome.
paper.abstract: Kallmann syndrome (KS) is a rare form of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) that causes delayed puberty and infertility, accompanied by a lifelong loss of smell. While hormone replacement therapy (HRT) restores standard hormone levels, the specific impact of an absent sense of smell on sexual relationships and desire remains largely unstudied. This study examined how lifelong smell loss shapes the psychosexual experiences of affected individuals. 38 adults were evaluated: 19 patients receiving stable HRT (10 with KS who lacked a sense of smell and 9 with CHH but normal smell) and 19 healthy matched individuals. Participants completed validated questionnaires assessing sexual desire, physical arousal, romantic behaviors, and attitudes toward intimacy. HRT effectively restored baseline sexual desire and general attitudes across all patients. However, individuals with KS reported significantly lower physical sexual arousal and engaged in far fewer sexual behaviors than those with an intact sense of smell. The lack of smell independently predicted lower arousal levels, despite patients maintaining normal mental desire and positive attitudes toward sex. These findings show that hormone therapy alone is insufficient to fully restore the sexual experience in KS. The lifelong absence of smell creates a distinct divide between mental desire and physical arousal, undermining sexual confidence and intimacy. Healthcare providers should therefore incorporate psychosexual counseling into routine clinical care to help patients navigate these sensory and emotional challenges.

paper.title: Identification of aversive aroma compounds that limit consumer acceptance of pea protein isolates using an integrated flavoromics approach.
paper.abstract: Pea protein isolates (PPIs) have emerged as sustainable plant-based protein ingredients; however, their widespread utilization remains constrained by undesirable off-flavors that limit consumer acceptance. This study aimed to identify the volatile compounds responsible for consumer disliking of commercial PPIs using an integrated flavoromics approach. A total of 39 aroma compounds were identified in an equal-proportion blend of 12 commercial PPI samples by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry/olfactometry. Targeted and untargeted volatile profiles were subsequently integrated with consumer aroma acceptance data using orthogonal partial least squares models. The addition of the five predictive compounds, methanethiol, methional, dimethyl disulfide, dimethyl trisulfide, and 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol, to a recombination model significantly reduced consumer aroma acceptance. Among these compounds, methanethiol and dimethyl trisulfide were identified as the primary drivers of consumer aroma disliking based on their strong predictive importance and odor activity values. Collectively, these findings establish sulfur-containing volatiles as the major contributors to lower consumer acceptance of commercial PPIs and provide mechanistic targets for flavor optimization to improve the marketability of pea protein-based foods.

paper.title: Intratemporal Anatomical Study of Facial Nerve in Cadaveric Bone in Nepal.
paper.abstract: Background The facial nerve courses in the intracranial, intratemporal and extratemporal regions. Intratemporal part of facial nerve is divided into meatal, labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid segments. Objective The objective of this study was to measure the length of tympanic segment of facial nerve, mastoid segment of facial nerve and distance between the second genu of facial nerve and origin of chorda tympani nerve. Method It was a descriptive study conducted from April 2025 till July 2025. A total of 65 temporal bones were dissected and the lengths of different segments of facial nerve were measured with a thread and millimetric scale. Result The mean length of tympanic segment of facial nerve was 7.86 ± 1.37 mm, which ranged from 5 mm to 11 mm. The length of mastoid segment of facial nerve ranged from 11 mm to 30 mm and its mean length was 16.84 ± 3.50 mm. The mean distance between the second genu of facial nerve to point of origin of chorda tympani nerve was found to be 12.87 ± 3.89 mm. This distance ranged from 2 mm to 24 mm. Conclusion There was a variability on anatomical measurements of different segments of facial nerve in the tympanomastoid compartment. This needs to be considered while performing middle ear and mastoid surgeries.

paper.title: Chest physiotherapy for pneumonia in children.
paper.abstract:
RATIONALE: Pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children aged under five years and remains a relevant cause of illness and death amongst older children and adolescents worldwide. Most pneumonia-related deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, where access to healthcare resources, diagnostic services, and supportive treatments may be more limited than in high-income settings. Chest physiotherapy is widely used as adjuvant treatment for pneumonia. Physiotherapy is thought to help remove inflammatory exudates, tracheobronchial secretions, and airway obstructions, and reduce airway resistance to improve breathing and enhance gas exchange. This is an update of a review first published in 2013 and updated in 2019.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy regarding time until clinical resolution in children (from birth to 18 years) of either gender with any type of pneumonia, irrespective of aetiology or clinical classification.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and PEDro and two clinical trial registries on 8 June 2026.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any type of chest physiotherapy with no chest physiotherapy (i.e. usual care for pneumonia treatment) in children with pneumonia. We did not apply any eligibility restrictions based on gestational age at birth.

OUTCOMES: Our critical outcomes were mortality, duration of hospital stay, and time to clinical resolution. Adverse events was an important outcome.

RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 1 tool for RCTs.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodological procedures. Two review authors independently selected studies for inclusion, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. For dichotomous outcomes, we calculated risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, we calculated mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. We synthesised the results for each outcome of interest using a random-effects meta-analysis. When pooling of data was not possible, we described the results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included six new RCTs (2304 children) in this update, for a total of 12 RCTs involving 2863 children aged from 29 days to 14 years with pneumonia who were treated as inpatients. Pneumonia severity was described as moderate in two trials, severe in five trials, and was not stated in five trials. The included studies were conducted in Bangladesh, Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Malawi, and South Africa. The studies assessed the effects of conventional (4 studies, 287 children), modern (1 study, 29 children), and instrumental chest physiotherapy (7 studies, 2547 children), comprising continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), bubble CPAP (bCPAP), and thoracic high-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) devices, compared to no chest physiotherapy. The studies were at overall low risk of bias. Blinding of participants was not possible in most studies, but we considered that the outcomes were unlikely to be influenced by the lack of blinding.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Six studies (2294 children) reported mortality. Three studies reported no deaths. However, three studies of bCPAP reported contrasting results: one reported higher mortality in the intervention group (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.27), whereas the other two found lower mortality in the bCPAP group (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.16; and RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.90). Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 83%; low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence suggests that chest physiotherapy results in little to no difference in mortality. Nine studies (2069 children) evaluated the duration of hospital stay. Five studies reported no difference between groups, whilst the other four studies found a shorter hospital stay in the group receiving chest physiotherapy. Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 88%; low-certainty evidence). Eleven studies (2219 children) assessed time to clinical resolution. Chest physiotherapy may result in little to no difference in time to clinical resolution of increased respiratory rate (MD -1.21, 95% CI -3.55 to 1.13; 4 studies, 1446 children; low-certainty evidence). Moreover, five studies reported the time to resolution of fever; however, pooling of data was not possible due to high heterogeneity (I² = 94%; very low-certainty evidence). Five studies assessed peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2), but pooling of data was not possible due to high heterogeneity (I² = 79%; very low-certainty evidence). Two out of five studies showed that children assigned to the intervention group had a significant increase in SpO2 compared to the control group. Regarding symptom improvement, three studies (336 children) found shorter cough and sputum duration in children receiving physiotherapy, whereas one study (89 children) observed a longer coughing period. Six studies (2382 children) reported adverse events. Most studies found no serious adverse events, but mild complications such as nasal irritation, skin breakdown, or abdominal distension were more common in children receiving CPAP or bCPAP. Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 80%; low-certainty evidence). Overall, the evidence was limited by small sample sizes, wide CIs, high risk of reporting bias, heterogeneity across interventions, and variations in outcome definitions. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to low.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: We could draw no reliable conclusions regarding the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy for children with pneumonia due to substantial variability in study characteristics and limitations in how data were presented and analysed across the included trials. Future research should ensure adequate methodological rigour, standardisation of physiotherapy techniques, appropriate outcome measures (such as duration of leukocytosis and airway clearance), and careful reporting of potential adverse effects.
